newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: E.Asia Oilseeds - Korean crushers to buy U.S. beans.
newsitem.headline: E.Asia Oilseeds - Korean crushers to buy U.S. beans.

text.p: South Korean soybean crushers are seen buying U.S. soybeans this week amid expectations prices will continue to come under pressure from forecasts for favourable crop weather in the Midwest, traders said on Monday.
They said local soybean crushers have also shown interest in South American origins, especially Brazilian soybeans, due to their more attractive prices.
"If U.S. soybeans remain at current levels or keep (their) current bearish trend, we expect some demand for U.S. soybean to appear soon," a trader with a South Korean crushing firm said.
He said Brazilian beans for July shipment were seen at a US$10 a tonne discount to U.S. origins despite the longer shipping period from the South American country.
Soybean futures prices on the Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) fell sharply on Friday with the July contract diving 10-1/4 U.S. cents to close at US$8.36 a bushel.

The Korean trader said the bearish trend in soybeans will continue for some time unless reversed by adverse weather forecasts. He said support for the CBOT July contract should emerge at between $8.32 to $8.33 a bushel.
But other dealers in Korea were concerned that prices may be bouncing back soon and expect a volatile weather market.

Traders said three major South Korean crushers have already covered their needs for July. Cheiljedang Corp and Shindongbang Corp have each bought 35,000-50,000 tonnes of soybeans while Sam Yang Foods Co Ltd purchased 15,000 tonnes of beans, they said.
South Korean soymeal buyers, however, were seen delaying fourth quarter buying on expectations Chicago futures prices would drop over the short-term, traders said.
"It's still too expensive to accelerate buying of U.S. soybeans," a senior official at a major edible oil maker said.
He said local end-users may consider buying if the spot July contract on the CBOT falls below the $8.00 a bushel level.
"Japanese crushers finished buying U.S. soybeans until July shipment, and are waiting for new crop," a soybean trader at a major trade house said. "They will remain quiet at least until August."
Some oilseed importers are considering importing Brazilian soybeans to cover their prompt requirements, traders said.
"The buyers are likely to delay their purchasing plans for soymeal (due to) expectations of lower soybean prices in the future," a trader with a Seoul-based foreign company said.
The trader said South Korean buyers have to cover their soymeal needs beginning in October.
"There has been no schedule for tenders to buy oilseeds and feeds up to now," he said.
In Japan, importers will probably not step up soybean buying, despite the falls in Chicago because they feel current prices remain too high, traders said.
